facts.text: Holds the collections of rare book dealers A. S. W. Rosenbach and his brother Philip H. Rosenbach.
Housed in two 19th-century townhouses at 2008-2010 Delancey Place near Rittenhouse Square.
The Rosenbach brothers lived at 2010 Delancey Place from 1926 to 1952.
Received a Pennsylvania state historical marker on April 2, 2008.
Established in 1999 in the Powelton Village neighborhood of West Philadelphia.
Shows works by artist Ellen Powell Tiberino along with works by her family members and friends.
Founded in 2011 as an arts gallery in Old City.
Highlights South Asian diasporic artistic voices through quarterly visual exhibitions and community events.
Started as a vision to open the basement of the Wolf Building as a space for free artistic expression.
Occupies 12,000 square feet with two rooms and a 650 capacity club.
Focuses mainly on live music and also hosts theater and fashion shows.
Houses installations by Philadelphia artists including Nosego, Adam Crawford and Todd Marrone.

name: Underground Railroad Museum at Belmont Mansion

facts.text: Tells the mansion's role in the Underground Railroad.
Mansion owner Judge Richard Peters was legal advisor to James Forten.
The Belmont Mansion property became part of Fairmount Park in 1869.
The only Colonial-themed post office operated by the United States Postal Service.
Still cancels stamps with the "B. Free Franklin" postmark.
The second-floor museum displays postal history and memorabilia.
Founded in 1855 by merchant and philanthropist William Wagner to offer free science courses.
Buildings were developed between 1859 and 1901 and present Wagner's collections in Victorian style.
Designated a National Historic Landmark for its architecture and state of preservation.
Occupies the former Cooper Library in Johnson Park, built in 1916.
Became a performance venue after the library closed, then was deeded to Rutgers University.
The front mosaic frieze, America Receiving the Gifts of Nations, was designed by D'Ascenzo Studios.
Added to the National Register of Historic Places on March 11, 1980.
Last home of poet Walt Whitman, who bought it in 1884 and died there in 1892.
The first home Whitman ever owned.
Sold to the city of Camden in 1921 and opened to the public in 1926.
Operated as a museum by the New Jersey Division of Parks and Forestry.
Located on the third floor of the Temple University School of Dentistry building.
Displays antique dental student teaching aids, including wax teeth carved by students.
Includes items of "Painless" Parker, such as a necklace of 357 teeth.

name: Weitzman National Museum of American Jewish History

facts.text: Smithsonian-affiliated museum on Independence Mall East at Market Street.
The 100,000-square-foot glass and terra-cotta building was designed by James Polshek.
The building opened to the public on November 26, 2010.
Includes an atrium, a Center for Jewish Education and a theater.
Built around 1756 by William Coleman as a summer residence.
David Franks added a second story and kitchen wing in 1772.
The city bought it in 1869 to add to Fairmount Park.
Opened as a house museum in 1930 and holds the Naomi Wood collection of antique household goods.
Specializes in contemporary prints, emerging artists and published editions.
Has operated in the Rittenhouse Square area since 1995.
Formerly the Thomas H. Kean New Jersey State Aquarium.
Reopened in its current form on May 25, 2005.
Home to about 8,000 animals in freshwater, marine and semi-aquatic habitats.
Opened December 5, 2006 as the Pearl Theatre at Avenue North, next to Temple University.
Named for the former Pearl Theatre on Ridge Avenue and in memory of entertainer Pearl Bailey.
AMC took over management in September 2016.
Has seven screens.
Opened on November 4, 2019 on the third floor of the Fashion District mall.
Has eight screens and 870 seats, with its own entrance at 11th and Filbert Streets.
The mall was formerly known as the Gallery.

name: Annenberg Center for the Performing Arts

facts.text: Founded in 1971 and owned by the University of Pennsylvania.
The facility was designed by Vincent G. Kling, who also designed the Philadelphia Mint.
Includes the Zellerbach Theatre and the Harold Prince Theatre.
Opened June 20, 1928 with the Warner Bros. film Old San Francisco.
Built and operated by local theatre owner Harry Fried, nicknamed "Fried's Folly".
Designed in the Art Deco style by architect William Harold Lee.
Named for Revolutionary War General Anthony Wayne.
Arden Theatre Company was formed in 1988.
Main property has the 175-seat Arcadia Stage and the 360-seat F. Otto Haas Stage.
The 100-seat Bob and Selma Horan Studio Theater is at 62 N 2nd Street in the Hamilton Family Arts Center.
Opened September 15, 1926 as the Egyptian Theatre with 1,450 seats.
Built in the Egyptian Revival style with terra cotta hieroglyphics, a charioteer and a phoenix on the facade.
Renamed the Bala in 1955 and converted to a triplex in 1995.
Founded in 1977 by Alfred Simpkins as an African-American professional theatre company.
Housed in the old Locust Street Theater, a former vaudeville house turned movie house.
The 428-seat space on 52nd Street is home to its resident ensemble.
Established a Walk of Fame honoring African Americans of stage, screen and television in 1996.
Part of the Ellen and Ronald Caplan Center for Performing Arts, which opened in September 2008.
Has 140 seats and sits on the upper floors of Terra Hall at 211 South Broad Street.
Black box theater with 100 seats in the Caplan Center for Performing Arts, opened in September 2008.
Located in Terra Hall at 211 South Broad Street.
Has six screens and 1,179 seats.
Cinemark took over the theater in June 2013.
Performs at The Adrienne Theater in the Rittenhouse section of Center City.
Flagship show is ComedySportz, a competitive improv comedy match.
Located in the University of the Arts Student Center at Broad and Pine Streets.
Refurbished with pink tones and gold details after the university bought the building in 2000.
Seats nearly 500 guests across main audience and balcony seating.
Located inside the National Constitution Center at 525 Arch Street.
Has a permanent stage and a capacity of 209 guests.
